newsitem.title: THAILAND: More pain seen for depressed Thai property sector.
newsitem.headline: More pain seen for depressed Thai property sector.

text.p: Thailand's depressed property sector should brace for mergers, takeovers and bankruptcies in the medium to longer term as it faces a growing liquidity crunch, analysts said on Wednesday.
Conditions in all sectors of the property market had deteriorated and a liquidity squeeze threatened even some of the sector's biggest firms, the analysts told Reuters.
Lofty Thai lending rates have raised financing costs for highly geared developers and slowed demand while oversupply has restrained land prices and rents in most sectors, they added.
"Aggressive expansion and land bank acquisition has been debt financed and that is the problem," said Wapan Wongpanit, property analyst at ING Barings.

"What I think will happen is that at some point in time, when companies cannot hold out any longer there will be a huge inventory draw down, and when that happens land prices will collapse," Wapan said.
"If things don't improve, a lot of property companies are going to go bust this year," he said.

Thai lenders, warned by the central bank to reduce real estate lending and already stung by rising non-performing loans in the sector are reluctant to extend lines of credit to developers, property firm executives said.

"I don't know how far away from unravelling the sector is ... but my feeling is that people who have exhausted their lines of credit may not survive this year intact," David Simister, managing director of property firm Richard Ellis Thailand, told Reuters.

"I think, like the finance sector, we will see mergers and exchange of assets, whether it will be Hong Kong or Singaporean groups taking a major stake in a property company in return for providing fresh credit, or whether it will be two companies first in the queue for new bonds remains to be seen," he said.

The Thai government on Tuesday approved a 100 billion baht ($3.85 billion) government bond issue to fund a buyout of some of the estimated 800 billion baht in loans Thai financiers have extended to the troubled sector.
That may limit damage to the financiers but cannot solve the real-estate sector's more fundamental problems, analysts said.

"There needs to be a broad solution to the problems developers face from oversupply, from lack of demand from buyers," said Supon Pronchokchai, managing director for of real estate research firm the Agency for Real Estate Affairs Ltd.

Goverment figures show there are more than 300,000 empty residential units in Bangkok and the oversupply problem is likely to worsen as the supply of new projects coming on line continues to outstrip demand, the analysts said.
Even if some of these new projects were to collapse it would be a good sign of rationalisation in the sector, they added.

"In an ideal world there may be no harm in one or two people who have very unviable schemes being brought to account," Simister said. "One of the real crises here is that built property here is very expensive against average income."
